form: The Long and Short of Subject Clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm* Gloria Mellesmoen University of Victoria Bailey Trotter University of British Columbia Abstract: There are long and short forms of indicative subject clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm. The choice between allomorphs is sensitive to: (i) whether there is a vowel in the phonological string to the left of the clitic, (ii) whether the future morpheme is to the right of the clitic, and (iii) if the clitic is part of a proclitic or enclitic string. We adopt a two-step approach to lexical insertion, showing that: (i) Insert must happen morpheme-by-morpheme, (ii) insertion rules can refer to phonological content in one direction and morphological features in the other direction, (iii) affixes and clitics must be part of the same spell-out domain in ʔayʔaǰuθəm, and (iv) allomorph selection within a spell-out domain must happen prior to building prosodic structure (i.e., before a cycle of phonology). Keywords: ʔayʔaǰuθəm, clitics, subject morphology, allomorphy, lexical insertion

Allomorph selection may be sensitive to both phonological and morphological information (see, e.g., Gouskova and Bobaljik 2019 and references therein). The types of phonological and morphological conditions that can affect the form of a single morpheme provide insight into the grammar and interfaces between its different components. For example, how much morphosyntactic information and phonological structure can be present at the same point in the derivation?

In this paper, we present an analysis of subject clitic allomorphy in ʔayʔaǰuθəm (a.k.a. Comox- Sliammon), showing that lexical insertion must proceed one morpheme at a time to allow for simultaneous morphosyntactic and phonological conditioning. ʔayʔaǰuθəm is a Central Salish language, traditionally spoken by the Tla’amin, Homalco, Klahoose, and K’ómoks communities along the Northern Georgia Strait in British Columbia. We build on the description of subject clitic allomorphy presented in Huijsmans (2023), who finds that both morphological and phono- logical factors condition allomorph choice. While she proposes the prosodic structure conditions the choice of allomorph, we argue that allomorph selection must happen before any prosodic structure is built. More generally, we predict that: (i) it is only possible to access phonological information from one direction and morphological information from the other, and (ii) allomorph selection during lexical insertion cannot be conditioned by derived prosodic structure. Empirical facts concerning short and long forms of indicative subject clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm are previewed in Section 2. Section 3 provides a summary of the analysis proposed in Huijsmans (2023), including the predictions that it makes (and which of these predictions are not borne out). We build on the insights from previous work and present an analysis in Section 4 that has implications related to spell-out, allomorph selection, and lexical insertion; the implications of our analysis are explored in Section 5. Section 6 concludes the paper.

Indicative subject clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm are second position clitics; they occur second in the clause following the predicate, as shown in (1), or the pre-predicative auxiliary if one is present, as shown in (2).1

form: Indicative subject clitics are used in main clauses with both transitive and instransitive pred- icates. In addition to the subject clitics, there are sixteen other second position clitics in ʔayʔa- ǰuθəm. These clitics form a morphological unit — the clitic string — and occur in a fixed order with respect to each other. Clitic allomorphy is conditioned both by properties of hosts (comprised of a root and any affixes) and neighbouring clitics. The 1SG.SBJ, 1PL.SBJ, and 2SG.SBJ clitics have both long and short allomorphs. These allomorphs are labeled as “full” and “reduced” forms in Huijsmans (2023); however, we use the terms long and short in this paper to avoid the implication that the short forms arise from a synchronic process of phonological reduction.2 The short allomorph of the first person singular subject is shown in (3), and the long allomorph is shown in (4).

form: 3 Previous Analysis: Conditioned by Prosodic Structure

Huijsmans (2023) adopts a two-step approach to lexical insertion (Svenonius and Bye 2012). Syntactic heads are first matched to morphological features at L-match; the phonological form then replaces these features at Insert.4 Clitics are linearised prior to allomorph selection. She proposes that the V, v, and Voice heads are spelled out as part of an earlier phase than the clitics. If the predicate undergoes a cycle of phonology without (and crucially before) the clitics are spelled out, then Huijsmans (2023) reasons that derived prosodic structure from this earlier cycle is available to condition allomorph selection. She argues that subject clitic allomorphy is sensitive to the prosodic weight of the clitic’s host; the long form is selected when the clitic is attached to a host that is otherwise too light to meet the minimal requirements for a well-formed prosodic word, while the short forms are used elsewhere.

3 Certain clitics in Nxaʔamxčín (Moses-Columbian) are flexible with respect to whether they precede or follow their host (Lyon and Czaykowska-Higgins 2020); these flexible clitics include subject markers. Unlike ʔayʔaǰuθəm, sequences of Nxaʔamxčín clitics show a mirrored order with respect to their host in proclitic sequences, i.e., subject clitics are always closest to the host. ʔayʔaǰuθəm clitics maintain the same linear ordering with respect to other clitics in both proclitic and enclitic strings.

A well-formed prosodic word must have at least one foot; feet in ʔayʔaǰuθəm are “optimally bimoraic” (Blake 2000:155). Schwas are epenthetic and non-moraic. In other words, schwas do not contribute phonological weight and are not present in the underlying form; their distribution is predictable based on the phonological grammar of the language (Blake 2000). All other vowels in the language are moraic and are typically present in the underlying form. Consonants are assigned weight by position (Hayes 1989): they are moraic when part of a coda, but non-moraic when part of an onset. The examples in (10) exemplify the relationship between underlying and surface forms with respect to which segments are moraic. A weak root that surfaces as CəC, e.g., [məq̓] ‘full’ in (10a), has no underlying vowels (e.g., /mq̓/). Schwa epenthesis provides a nucleus. However, these forms are monomoraic because only the coda consonant is assigned a mora. In contrast, the vowel in a strong root, such as huǰ- 'finish' in (10b), is underlying and is assigned a mora; CVC roots are bimoraic because the vowel and coda consonant are each assigned a mora.5

Huijsmans (2023) proposes that a single monomoraic foot does not meet the phonological requirements for a minimal prosodic word. Accordingly, the monomoraic word from (10a) cannot be parsed into a well-formed prosodic word, while the bimoraic word from (10b) can be.6 This difference is summarised in (11).

A prosodic word is therefore optionally built following spell-out of the phase containing the clitic’s host and a subsequent cycle of phonology. Huijsmans (2023) argues that the short form of a subject clitic is selected when it attaches to a prosodic word (if one was built during the previous cycle of phonology); the long form is inserted elsewhere. The choice of allomorph depends on whether the predicate met the criteria for a well-formed prosodic word prior to the addition of the clitics. A weak root like [məq̓] must take the long form of the subject clitic because it is too light to be parsed into a well-formed foot (and therefore does not meet the minimal requirements for a prosodic word). In contrast, [huy] is bimoraic, which means it can be parsed into a well-formed binary foot and word; the short form is inserted. Huijsmans (2023) extends this analysis to the /tᶿ/ form of the first person singular subject: this form is chosen if the clitic meets the phonological criteria for the short form but is followed by the future clitic. Her lexical entry for 1SG.SBJ is summarised in (12).

Huijsmans (2023) finds that only clitics that originate higher than the clausal demonstratives can appear as proclitics. The presence of a proclitic clausal demonstrative conditions the selection of proclitic allomorph of a subject clitic. She proposes that: (i) proclisis is associated with specific allomorphs, and (ii) only clitics with a proclitic allomorph may occur as part of a proclitic string.

The analysis proposed in Huijsmans (2023) accounts for the general pattern of subject clitic allomorphy: the long form is typically attested with weak roots (and no/few suffixes), while the short form is found whenever a word has a strong root. Further, it accounts for the fact that allomorphy is conditioned by both phonological and morphological factors. However, the specific implementation of the analysis and reference to prosodic structure makes a number of predictions that are not borne out.

Huijsmans (2023) must assume that complex codas are always monomoraic, regardless of whether they arise from affixation or their size (i.e., number of segments). This means that complex codas are equally as heavy as simplex ones, which is a departure from previous work on the phonology of the language. For example, Blake (2000:159--162) argues that CV- form of diminutive reduplication occurs with CVC words because the typical -C- form would create a superheavy syllable (σµµµ). If only a single mora was associated with multiple coda consonants, then there would be no difference between CVC and CVCC syllables.

In addition to predictions about complex codas, the prosodic word approach makes predic- tions about open CV syllables. The word ho ‘go’ is a monomoraic word because it has a moraic vowel and no coda; it has the same weight as a closed syllable with a schwa (e.g., məq̓ ‘full’). While the long form is predicted for monomoraic words, the example in (15) shows that ho takes the short form.

form: Finally, if subject allomorphy is conditioned prosodic structure, then the short form of a clitic should surface on any word with C1C2 reduplication. Plural C1C2 reduplication always adds a monomoraic closed syllable to a word (Mellesmoen 2025:172). If allomorph selection is based on whether a bimoraic foot can be built, then applying C1C2 reduplication will always yield a well- formed prosodic word. However, the long form is found when C1C2 reduplication is combined with a weak root, as shown in (16). Reduplication does not influence the choice of allomorph, despite providing the perfect phonological repair (i.e., doubling a monomoraic syllable).

form: The patterns with complex codas (resulting from triconsonantal weak roots and words with consonant affixes), open monomoraic syllables, and reduplication pose problems for the analysis in Huijsmans (2023). However, the fact that her description and generalizations hold for a large portion of the data indicates that the problem is likely with the specific implementation, rather than the overall inspiration behind the analysis. The examples in this section suggest that the subject clitics cannot be sensitive to derived prosodic structure (including moraic codas and prosodic words); however, the example with the question clitic =a in (5a) provides an example where the presence of a moraic vowel does trigger the short form.7 The timing of spell-out, lexical insertion, and cycles through the phonological grammar pose challenges for the analysis in Huijsmans (2023). These challenges suggest that allomorph selection for clitics must happen before any prosodic structure is built; our analysis in the following section builds on the insights from Huijsmans (2023) with modifications to the theoretical model and assumptions.

We adopt a span-based approach to spell-out (Svenonius 2016). In order to derive the correct position and form of clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm, the spell-out domain must include the span of heads from V up to the highest head in the clitic string: root, affixes, auxiliaries, and clitics must be part of the same spell-out domain. This assumption is a departure from Huijsmans (2023), as well as other previous work on ʔayʔaǰuθəm (see Section 5.1 for arguments against the vP as a phase in Huijsmans 2023 and the w-span as a spell-out domain in Mellesmoen 2025).

7 Huijsmans (2023) must stipulate that a cycle of phonology is triggered each time a clitic is inserted, otherwise the question clitic could not be parsed into a prosodic word; it can only affect the form of the subject clitic if it has already undergone a cycle of phonology with the host.
Indicative subject marking is introduced in InflP; the tree in (17) shows the syntactic position of InflP relative to the clitics that affect its shape (i.e., the question and future markers).8

We adopt a two-step model of lexical insertion (Svenonius and Bye 2012), paired with an feature-driven approach to linearisation (Huijsmans 2023; Davis and Huijsmans 2024). The first step of lexical insertion is L-match: terminal elements in the syntax are matched with lexical entries by their features. Lexical entries include features (e.g., [suffix]) that provide instructions for linearisation. Linearisation happens prior to the insertion of phonological content. Linearisa- tion starts at the lowest head in the span and moves upward. Heads with the [suffix] feature are linearised to the right of the head (or string of heads) beneath them in the span; heads that bear the [enclitic] feature are linearised to the right of the head above them, forming a clitic string. The highest head with the [enclitic] feature will attach downward to the closest head (or string of heads) because there is no head above it. The head or string of heads directly beneath the clitic string will invariably correspond to the predicate or the predicate auxiliary.

Linearisation for the sentence in (18) is shown in (19). Glosses (e.g., 2SG.SBJ) are used as a placeholder for the relevant morphological features matched during the first step of lexical insertion. Linearisation starts from V, which the lowest head in the span. The next highest head is v, which is linearised to the right of V because it bears the [suffix] feature. In other words, v is linearised relative to V (= V-v). The subject marker has an [enclitic] feature, which means it is linearised to the right of the head above it (= Force-Infl), forming a clitic string. There is no head above the question marker, so it must be linearised relative to the string of heads beneath it (= [V-v]-[Force-Infl]).

Insert, the second step of lexical insertion, occurs following linearisation. Phonological content replaces the morphological features at Insert. Subject clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm are sen- sitive to both phonological and morphological information. We propose that Insert proceeds one morpheme at a time, such that allomorphy can be sensitive to the phonological shape of morphemes already inserted and the morphological features of morphemes not yet inserted. This is exemplified in (20), the feature bundles in the linearised string in (20a) are replaced with phonological content, one at time.

In ʔayʔaǰuθəm, phonological content must be inserted from left to right because allomorphy is conditioned by phonological form to the left of the clitic and morphological features to the right. The relevant phonological material is a linear string (prior to building prosodic structure). Schwa is epenthetic in ʔayʔaǰuθəm; it is not present in the underlying form. Therefore, we propose that /tᶿ/ is inserted if there is a vowel in the phonological string (to the left) and the future morpheme follows (to the right), /č/ is inserted if there is a vowel in the string (and no future morpheme), and /čan/ is inserted elsewhere.

The lexical entry for 1SG.SBJ is provided in (21). The Elsewhere Principle, proposed by Halle and Marantz (1993), applies at Insert (Huijsmans 2023:41). The most specified form is selected over all others if its conditions are met. /tᶿ/ allomorph is inserted when there is a vowel somewhere in the phonological string to the left and the future morpheme is directly to the right; /č/ allomorph is inserted when the phonological condition is met but the future morpheme does not follow the subject marker. /čan/ is inserted everywhere else.

When the subject markers are in a proclitic string, they are always in the short form. Huijs- mans (2023:80) highlights that specific allomorphs must be selected when a morpheme surfaces as a proclitic. Linearisation features are morphological features; they are present until phonological content is inserted. Proclitic and enclitic forms of the subject clitics can therefore be distinguished by linearisation features ([proclitic] vs. [enclitic]). Given that the default position of subject clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm is enclitic, only [proclitic] needs to be specified in the vocabulary insertion rules. There is only one possible allomorph that corresponds to [1SG.SBJ, proclitic], as shown in (22). We discuss markedness, default allomorphs, and the subject clitics further in Section 5.3.

If linearisation features were not available at Insert, the long form of a subject clitic should always be selected in a proclitic string, given that it will be the leftmost morpheme in the string; there will not be a vowel in the phonological string to meet the conditions for the short form. This provides further evidence for the utility of morphological linearisation features: they also play a role in allomorph selection.
In conclusion, subject clitic allomorphy is determined by a combination of factors: position, preceding segments, and following morpheme. Allomorph choice at Insert is summarized in Figure 1.

Further discussion of this pattern and possible analyses can be found in Huijsmans (2023) and Trotter (2025). An analysis of this pattern is beyond the scope of this paper.

Clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm provide insight into the process of allomorph selection and lexical insertion, as well as the relationship between different components of the grammar. The analysis presented in Section 4 has implications for when spell-out and phonological processes apply (Section 5.1), when different types of allomorphy are possible (Section 5.2), what assumptions must be made about markedness and default allomorphy (Section 5.3), and which types of information are available at the second step of lexical insertion (Section 5.4).

The short form of a subject clitic is inserted if a vowel is present in the string of segments to its left. Our analysis predicts that schwas should not influence subject clitic allomorphy because they are epenthetic; they are not present in the underlying form, but they are inserted during the phonological derivation to ensure well-formed syllables, feet, and words (see Blake 2000). The data presented in Section 3.2 shows that only underlying (i.e., non-schwa) vowels affect clitic allomorphy, such as the vowels in strong roots or the question clitic. Our approach correctly predicts that subject clitic allomorphy is therefore crucially dependent on the phonological shape of underlying forms, which means that clitics must be part of the same spell-out domain as affixes in ʔayʔaǰuθəm.

If clitics were part of a separate spell-out domain from affixes, then we would expect the choice of allomorph to be based on surface form phonology (as in Huijsmans 2023), rather than underlying forms. If the root and affixes are spelled out separately from the clitics, then they undergo a cycle of phonology before the clitics are added. Huijsmans (2023) proposes that a prosodic word is built during this cycle of phonology if there are at least two moras, which means that well-formed prosodic words cannot be built for roots that surface as CəC. The choice between the long and short from of a subject clitic is then determined by whether or not it is attaching to a prosodic word. However, this analysis makes the wrong predictions for a word like ho ‘go’ (23), which takes the short form despite having a single mora, and a word like pəɬtsxʷ ‘make thick’ (24), which takes the long form despite having multiple coda consonants (which would meet the minimum for a bimoraic word).

form: 9 Huijsmans (2023) assumes that only the outermost head in a phase is still visible at the next stage of the derivation. Even if the underlying form of one morpheme was still accessible, the subject clitic needs to see underlying forms for every morpheme to its left.

Following a cycle of phonology, it is no longer possible to refer to the underlying form. If the definition refers to vowels (or nuclei), then schwa cannot be distinguished from other vowels. If the definition refers to moras and prosodic structure, then CəCC and CVC words should both take the short form; CəC and CV words should both take the long form. It is only possible to group CəCC with CəC and CVC with CV if allomorph selection happens prior to phonology.9 The fact that allomorph selection for clitics must happen before word-level phonology also poses problems for models that separate affixes and clitics into separate domains (e.g., word vs. phrase; lexical vs. post-lexical). Mellesmoen (2025) proposes that word (defined as a w-span in the sense of Svenonius 2016) is a spell-out domain. Under her analysis, all word-level phonology, including reduplication, happens before the clitics are present. This approach makes the wrong predictions for the subject clitics: the long form would therefore be expected in any word where reduplication adds a vowel; however, reduplication does not affect the choice of allomorph.

form: Clitics must be part of the same spell-out domain as affixes in ʔayʔaǰuθəm because allomorph selection must happen before any cycle of phonological evaluation, otherwise the phonology will introduce additional vowels and moras that would meet the conditions for short form where the long form is attested.

The amount and type of syntactic, morphological, and phonological information available varies across different components of the grammar. The available information constrains the types of allomorphy possible at different points in the derivation.

Working within similar theoretical frameworks to the present paper, Mellesmoen (2025) and Davis (in press) each differentiate between allomorph selection at Insert and during the phonological derivation. Both analyses propose a strong restriction on the type of allomorphy possible during the phonological derivation: morphological information cannot play a role in allomorph selection during the phonological derivation. This restriction follows from the fact that morphological features are replaced at Insert with phonological content; they are not accessible when applying phonological rules or considering phonological constraints. The only possible allomorphy during the phonological derivation is phonologically conditioned.

Mellesmoen (2025) and Davis (in press) make different predictions about the type of allo- morphy that is possible at Insert. Davis (in press) proposes a strong restriction on allomorphy at Insert: allomorph selection sensitive to morphosyntactic features must happen at Insert, while phonological conditioning can only happen at the point where the clitic is parsed into prosodic structure. Under this analysis, all phonologically conditioned allomorphy must happen during the phonological derivation. In contrast, Mellesmoen (2025) proposes a weak restrictions on allomorphy at Insert. She argues that morphological conditioning is only possible at Insert, while certain types of phonological conditioning (i.e., those that do not refer to derived prosodic structure) are also possible at Insert.

form: The subject clitics show both phonological and morphological conditioning. Under the strong restrictions proposed by Davis (in press), a set of listed allomorphs {tᶿ, čan} must be selected at Insert if followed by the future marker, while the set {č, čan} is selected otherwise. The phonological grammar must then select between the long and the short form (see Mascaró 2007 for discussion of listed allomorphs). However, this approach faces the same challenges as in Huijsmans (2023) because choice of allomorph must depend on the underlying form. The choice between the long and short form cannot be determined during the phonological derivation because it will not be possible to distinguish between CV and CəC and CVC and CəCC.

The choice between the three allomorphs must happen at Insert, which means that some phonological information must be available, which is consistent with the weak restrictions pro- posed by Mellesmoen (2025). Allomorphy sensitive to prosodic structure must therefore involve either: (i) late allomorph selection in the phonology (i.e., listed allomorphs) or (ii) reference to prosodic structure in the underlying form (e.g., a foot in the UR for lexical stress). There are still a number of questions that must be explored if phonologically-conditioned allomorphy is possible both at Insert and during the phonological derivation. For example, how are phonological conditions evaluated when a set of listed allomorphs is provided at Insert? For example, the form of the active intransitive is -ʔəm or -aʔam: -aʔam is used following sequences of two or more consonants. The active intransitive must involve late allomorph selection (i.e., listed allomorphs) because the choice of allomorph is influenced by reduplication, as shown in (27) and (28). Reduplication does not happen until the phonological derivation.

form: The example in (27) above has no underlying vowels; we expect that it should take the long form of a subject clitic. However, we have recorded some variation between the long and the short form in our elicitation. While this might represent a reanalysis or uncertainty regarding a possible underlying vowel in the -ʔəm form of the active intransitive, it may also provide insight into phonologically-conditioned allomorph selection if two options (one with a vowel and one without) are visible at Insert. If variation emerges because multiple options are available, this would have significant implications for our understanding of allomorphy, as well as the theoretical framework outlined in the paper. We leave this as a question for future elicitation and research.

Our analysis also proposes that the long forms of subject enclitics are inserted as the default (i.e., least specified) form; this conclusion is consistent with Huijsmans (2023). Designating the long form as the “elsewhere” form follows from the fact that insertion rules are written based on the presence of phonological or morphological content, rather than the absence (i.e., having no vowel to its left).

At first glance, positing the long forms as the elsewhere condition may appear counterintuitive with respect to markedness. The short forms are more common than the long ones; they appear with a greater number of roots and combinations of morphemes. Further, a root that would take the long form on its own will often take the short form when affixes with underlying (i.e., non- schwa) vowels are present. Examples of the same root taking both allomorphs are given in (29) and (30), respectively.

form: The short form is also less restricted with respect to position because it can occur as both a proclitic or an enclitic, while the long form is restricted to the enclitic string. The default allomorph is more limited in distribution and frequency than allomorphs that are specified for particular phonological and morphological environments.

When morphosyntactic and phonological factors are considered separately, there is additional support for our analysis. First, different types (and amounts) of allomorphy are expected for unmarked terms when compared to marked ones in morphology. Specifically, marked terms are expected to have simpler allomorphy patterns than unmarked ones (Waugh and Lafford 2008). Only one of the linearisation features ([proclitic] or [enclitic]) needed to be specified in Section 4 to predict the correct forms. If we treat [proclitic] as the marked case, which is consistent with the fact that all clitics may be enclitics but only certain ones (and in certain combinations) may be proclitics, then we get the vocabulary insertion rules in (31). As the marked term, there is a single choice at Insert for a proclitic; the enclitic represents the unmarked condition, which is consistent with the fact that it tolerates increased complexity with respect to phonologically-conditioned and morphologically-conditioned allomorphy.

Second, the morphological environment (presence of the future marker) is only relevant if the word meets the phonological criteria for the short form of the clitic. The long form of the subject clitic is attested across future and non-future contexts. If the short form were the default, then two separate vocabulary insertion rules would be needed to account for words that would otherwise meet the phonological conditions for /čan/, but the morphological conditions for /tᶿ/, as shown in (32). Therefore, with respect to morphological conditioning, the long form is truly unmarked.

form: Finally, we note that the long forms of the subject clitics are older than the short ones. For example, the long form of the first person enclitic =čan is cognate with subject markers across the family, such as =čən in Sechelt (Beaumont 1985) and =(ɬ)kan in St'át'imcets (Van Eijk 1997). The short form in ʔayʔaǰuθəm is conditioned by phonological shape; therefore it may have emerged first through phonological reduction (e.g., deletion of a vowel: čaxʷ → čxʷ). If this allomorphy first emerged as an innovation in the phonological grammar, then this process has since undergone lexicalization (Ramsammy 2015): the lexical entry for the morpheme has since been restructured to reflect the output of the original phonological process.

The innovation of the short form =č must predate the development of the morphologically- conditioned form =tᶿ. Davis (1978:227) proposes that /tᶿ/ comes from an earlier sequence of /čs/; the /č/ comes from the short form of the subject clitic and /s/ comes from the future clitic =səm. The short form therefore represents an earlier change, which then created the /čs/ sequence that lead to the development of =tᶿ for the future.10 If this historical trajectory is correct, then the default form represents the oldest form in the language, while the other allomorphs are the product of reanalysis based on the output of previous phonological processes. It is therefore unsurprising that the long forms are the least marked case, even if they appear to be more marked on the basis of synchronic distribution.

There is some variation with respect to the choice of allomorph that deserves further study. It is unclear how much of this variation should be characterized as free variation or non-linguistic sources (i.e., uncertainty or error), as we note variation across sources, speaker, and lexical items. Impressionistically, we note that the long form is often supplied with words where the short form is expected; there are fewer cases where a short form is used on a word where a long form is required. This would be consistent with the long form being the elsewhere case, as it shows the fewest phonological and morphological restrictions. However, we leave this variation as a topic for future research.

The correct allomorph of subject clitics in ʔayʔaǰuθəm requires information about the phonological form of one morpheme and about the morphological identity of another. Phonological form is only accessible once it has been inserted; morphological features are not present following Insert. The subject clitics therefore provide evidence that the second step of lexical insertion must proceed one morpheme at time, such that the Insert is able to see phonological content in one direction (in the linear string) and morphological information in the other. In other words, Insert cannot apply to all morphemes in the string in a single parallel step; Insert must proceed morpheme-by- morpheme.

10 We give this allomorph as =tᶿ for consistency with Huijsmans (2023), though we assume that the relevant allomorph is =tᶿəm, which represents either a portmanteau of the subject and the future or is followed by a null future marker.

Our analysis is similar to Huijsmans (2023) in that Insert can refer to either phonological or morphological information. However, her analysis assumes that a cycle of phonology is triggered following Insert for each morpheme. We assume that both stages of lexical insertion precede any cycle of word-level phonology. This limits the type of phonological information that may factor into allomorph selection at Insert since it is restricted to the string of segments available in the underlying form. Prosodic structure that would be built up over the prosodic word is therefore not available at the point of allomorph selection. Any allomorphy that is sensitive to syllable or foot structure must happen later (i.e., with listed allomorphs or prosodic affixes that trigger non-concatenative morphology).

Insert in ʔayʔaǰuθəm proceeds one morpheme at a time from left to right. It is plausible that there are languages where this process moves in the opposite direction (i.e., right to left), or where Insert starts at the root and moves outward. Brown and Davis (2024) describe an interrogative clitic =du in Sm'algyax, a Coast Tsimshian language, with morphological conditioning on the left side: there is a =yu allomorph that is only possible following a wh-word. This suggests that Insert in Sm'algyax does not follow the same path or direction as in ʔayʔaǰuθəm. In fact, there is also evidence of phonological conditioning from the right side. The forms =du and =yu only appear if phonological material follows; if they are final in the phonological string, then =da or =ya are used instead. Davis (p.c.) notes that =da or =ya are also used where a null pronoun follows the clitic, which means this allomorphy cannot be not morphologically conditioned. Morphemes to the right of the interrogative clitic must be inserted first in order for a null morpheme (i.e., absence of phonological structure) to be indistinguishable from being the final morpheme in the linearised string.

Regardless of whether Insert proceeds left-to-right or right-to-left, the predictions about allo- morph selection are the same. By hypothesis, Insert can only be sensitive to phonological form on one side and morphological features on the other; this sensitivity should be consistent with a systematic order of application of Insert across morphemes in a linearised string within a given language. We leave this as an area for further research.

Subject clitic allomorphy in ʔayʔaǰuθəm provides insight into theories of allomorph selection, as well as the architecture of the grammar. We build on the analysis in Huijsmans (2023), but ultimately argue against her proposal that clitic allomorphy is sensitive to the prosodic structure of the clitic’s host. An analysis of subject clitic allomorphy based on prosodic structure: (i) makes incorrect predictions about the distribution of short and long subject markers, and (ii) requires prosodic information to be accessible to the derivation at lexical insertion. The choice of allomorph must be based on the underlying vowel, which means that clitics must be spelled out within the same phase as affixes in ʔayʔaǰuθəm. Further, the combination of phonological and morphological conditions at Insert provides evidence that insertion happens one morpheme at time; in ʔayʔaǰuθəm this is from left to right. Future work is needed to explore variation in allomorph choice, as well as the larger theoretical and typological implications raised by this study.
